title: Word Search II
description:
You are given an `m x n` grid `board` of lowercase letters and a list of distinct `words`. Return every word that can be traced on the board by starting at any cell and moving to a horizontally or vertically adjacent cell at each step. A cell may be used **at most once per word**.

Each found word should appear once in the result, in any order.

examples.explanation: "oath" runs o(0,0) a(0,1) t(1,1) h(2,1). "eat" runs e(1,3) a(1,2) t(1,1). There is no 'p' on the board, and the 'r' is not adjacent to an 'a'.
The second 'b' would reuse the cell at (0,1).

constraints: All words are distinct; board and words contain only lowercase letters.
hints: Running the single-word backtracking search once per word repeats the same board walks over and over.
Put all the words in a trie and do one DFS from each cell, advancing through the trie as you move on the board. Stop as soon as the current prefix is not in the trie.
Record a word when you reach its end node, then remove it from the trie (and prune empty nodes) so it is reported once and dead branches are not re-explored.
signature: def findWords(self, board: List[List[str]], words: List[str]) -> List[str]:
approach:
**Search the board once for all words at the same time by walking a trie alongside the DFS.** Insert every word into a trie. From each cell, start a backtracking DFS that only continues into a neighbour whose letter is a child of the current trie node. Whenever the current node carries a complete word, add it to the output.

**Two optimisations that make it fast in practice:**
1. *Report each word once* by removing its end marker the first time it is reached, instead of using a result set.
2. *Prune the trie* as you backtrack: when a node has no children left (all its words were found), delete it from its parent. Later DFS calls never enter that subtree. On the all-'a' board this is the difference between finishing instantly and never finishing.

**Why it works:** every path on the board that spells a prefix of some word corresponds to a path in the trie from the root. Walking both together means a board path is abandoned the moment it stops being a prefix of any remaining word. Marking cells with a sentinel and restoring them on the way back enforces the use-once rule.

**Common mistakes:** running Word Search I once per word (O(words * cells * 4^L), times out at 3 * 10^4 words); forgetting to restore the cell after the DFS; returning duplicate words; forgetting that a word can be a prefix of another, so you must keep searching past an end node.

**Interview follow-ups:** why a trie and not a hash set of prefixes (a set works too, but the trie gives O(1) per step and enables pruning); how to handle diagonal moves or wraparound; estimate the worst-case complexity and explain what pruning buys; make it incremental when words are added later.

complexity.time: O(m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1)) worst case, L = max word length; far less with pruning
